patch_json: {"reader_guide":{"takeaway":"Prefer B, complete temporary-file preparation followed by os.replace, when preserving a complete checkpoint during updates matters. This conclusion is conditional on complete preparation and successful replacement on the destination mount. A, direct truncating rewrite, remains reasonable when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Neither candidate has an established power-loss durability guarantee; the recommendation remains provisional pending independent review.","purpose":"Help a developer choose how one process updates a JSON checkpoint: a saved state file used to resume work. Compare direct rewriting with preparing a separate complete file before publishing it.","scope":"Two frozen candidates, A and B, for a single-process JSON checkpoint. Assume an existing complete checkpoint, a distinct temporary file for B, and no subsequent mutation of the published file. This is a source-grounded design comparison with zero experiments. No implementation, interruption outcome, latency, failure rate or filesystem-specific persistence was tested.","comparison_exception":"The frozen target is five methods, but the requirements expressly request only these two mechanisms. Adding three alternatives would expand the narrow checkpoint question rather than strengthen its comparison.","walkthrough":"Concrete with/without example, explicitly unmeasured: checkpoint.json initially contains {\"step\":10}; the next state is {\"step\":11}. Without separate publication, A truncates checkpoint.json and writes the new JSON directly. An interruption after truncation or after writing only {\"step\": can leave empty or incomplete content. This is reasoning from the specified mechanism, not an observed failure or a guarantee supplied by the two named passages. With separate publication, B writes the new JSON to a distinct temporary file in the destination directory and closes it before replacement. During preparation, the existing checkpoint is not being rewritten. Conditional on complete preparation and successful os.replace, the destination publishes the prepared file. Python documents successful replacement as atomic and warns of cross-filesystem failure. [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace). Linux documents destination replacement without a missing-path interval; it also leaves open descriptors unaffected. Existing readers can therefore retain their old file, an inference rather than a tested reader outcome. Linux EXDEV excludes different mounts, even mounts of the same filesystem. Place the temporary file on the destination mount, preferably in its directory; this condition alone does not ensure success. Treat replacement errors as failures, and do not describe a copy fallback as atomic replacement. [Linux rename(2), DESCRIPTION and EXDEV](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html). Figure F1 compares the two update paths; F2 expands B's publication boundary. Neither figure measures behavior.","glossary":"Checkpoint: saved application state for resuming work. Preparation: writing the complete new JSON before publication. Publication: making the prepared file available at the checkpoint pathname. Atomicity: the successful replacement has one indivisible pathname transition; preceding writes remain separate. Durability: persistence after power loss or system crash, which is unknown here. Mount: the filesystem attachment boundary relevant to Linux EXDEV.","limitations":"No measured outputs exist to reuse: the saved dossier has empty metrics, measured_thresholds, experiment_receipts and independent_grades. This reader's direct Linux access also returned Internal Error; the decisive original-page DESCRIPTION and EXDEV text was accessible through indexed retrieval. That access does not replace or repair the saved failed receipts. Independent review remains pending; this reader guide supplies no grade or acceptance. Atomic publication and file closure do not establish crash persistence or a complete synchronization protocol from the named passages. Actual interruption behavior, runtime costs and filesystem-specific effects remain unmeasured.
